# Overview & Orientation {background-color="#0f172a"}

## Executive Summary {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
### The Reproducibility Paradox in Physiology
- **Common Experimental Paradigm**: Cell physiology experiments routinely compare two or more groups (e.g., wild-type vs. transgenic, control vs. heart failure, diabetic vs. healthy).
- **The Pervasive Pitfall**: Multiple cells are isolated from a modest number of animals, and statistical tests (t-tests or ANOVA) are performed treating **each cell as an independent sample** ($N \times n$).
- **The "More Means Less" Paradox**: Naively measuring more cells per animal actually **inflates the false-positive rate** (up to 47% or higher under the null hypothesis!).

::: {.callout-note}
### Core Insight (Eisner 2021)
"Treating cells from the same animal as independent biological replicates violates the fundamental independence assumption of standard parametric tests, producing spurious statistical significance out of thin air."
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
<div class="stat-card">
  <div class="stat-number">47%</div>
  <div class="stat-label">Peak False-Positive Rate</div>
  <div class="stat-desc">Observed in simulations under the null hypothesis when cell variance is small relative to animal variance.</div>
</div>

<div class="stat-card">
  <div class="stat-number">N &times; n &rarr; N</div>
  <div class="stat-label">Effective Sample Size Collapse</div>
  <div class="stat-desc">As intraclass correlation (ICC) approaches 1.0, effective biological sample size collapses to animal count $N$.</div>
</div>

<div class="stat-card">
  <div class="stat-number">1984</div>
  <div class="stat-label">Hurlbert's Landmark Definition</div>
  <div class="stat-desc">Stuart Hurlbert defined pseudoreplication as using inferential statistics to test for treatment effects with replicates that are not independent.</div>
</div>
:::
:::

# The Pseudoreplication Crisis {#the-crisis background-color="#0f172a"}

## What is Pseudoreplication? {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### The Formal Definition
- Coined by **Stuart Hurlbert (1984)** in ecological field experiments:
  > *"The use of inferential statistics to test for treatment effects with data from replicates that are not statistically independent."*
- In laboratory physiology and biomedicine:
  - **Biological Unit ($N$)**: The animal, patient, or independent biological preparation.
  - **Technical Replicate ($n$)**: Multiple cells, tissue slices, wells, patches, or organelle traces sampled from that same biological unit.
- **The Core Violation**: A standard Student's t-test or ANOVA assumes all observations are independent and identically distributed ($\text{i.i.d.}$).
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### The Limiting Case ($N = 1, n = 100$)
- Imagine testing whether blood pressure differs between residents of London and New York.
- **Flawed Protocol**: Pick **one** Londoner and measure her blood pressure 100 times; pick **one** New Yorker and measure his blood pressure 100 times.
- With $n = 100$, standard error is:
  $$\text{SE} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\sqrt{100}} = 0.1 \times \text{SD}$$
- Even a trivial difference between the two individuals produces $p < 0.0001$!
- **Error**: The test compares *these two specific individuals*, not the two cities!

::: {.callout-caution}
### The Physiology Parallel
Studying 3 animals with 10 cells each ($N \times n = 30$) is conceptually identical: it tests differences between the isolations, not the biological conditions.
:::
:::
:::

## Ubiquity Across Experimental Physiology {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Pervasive in High-Impact Literature
Studies across top cardiovascular, neuroscience, and endocrinology journals frequently pool sub-samples:
- **Cardiomyocyte Physiology**:
  - Measuring action potentials or Ca2+ transients from 5–20 myocytes per heart.
  - Recording hundreds of Ca2+ sparks per single myocyte (Sikkel et al., 2017).
- **Neuroscience & Slice Electrophysiology**:
  - Recording synaptic potentials from multiple neurons or dendritic spines per brain slice (Lazic, 2010).
- **Islet Biology & Diabetes**:
  - Assaying insulin secretion from multiple islets isolated per mouse (Attie & Yandell, 2026).
- **Cell Culture & Molecular Biology**:
  - Treating multiple wells or coverslips from the same cell line passage as independent (Lazic et al., 2018).
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Why Do Researchers Do It?
::: {.incremental}
1. **Cost & Animal Welfare (3Rs)**: Animals are expensive, ethically constrained, and labor-intensive to house and treat.
2. **Technical Yield**: Once an animal is sacrificed and cells isolated, collecting 10–20 cells from that prep takes marginal extra effort.
3. **Naïve Statistical Intuition**: Researchers mistakenly believe that "larger sample size ($N \times n$) always increases precision and reduces error."
4. **Software Defaults**: Standard spreadsheet and plotting software default to flat column t-tests without warning about nested structures.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
### The Consequence
A vast proportion of published physiological differences between wild-type and transgenic animals are likely **irreproducible false positives**.
:::
:::
:::

# Variance Sources & The ICC Framework {#icc-framework background-color="#0f172a"}

## Partitioning Two Sources of Variation {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Biological vs. Measurement Variation
In any hierarchical physiological experiment, total observed variance ($\sigma^2_{\text{total}}$) decomposes into two independent components:

$$\sigma^2_{\text{total}} = \sigma^2_{\text{animal}} + \sigma^2_{\text{cell}}$$

1. **Between-Animal Variance ($\sigma^2_{\text{animal}}$, $\text{SD}_{\text{animal}}$)**:
   - Genuine inter-individual biological differences (genetics, epigenetic state, age, physiological baseline).
   - Day-to-day experimental batch effects (temperature, perfusion solutions, enzymatic digestion quality, isolation stress).
2. **Within-Animal / Intra-Cell Variance ($\sigma^2_{\text{cell}}$, $\text{SD}_{\text{cell}}$)**:
   - Technical measurement noise (instrument precision, electrode seal, optical focus).
   - Intrinsic cellular heterogeneity within the same organ.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### The Limiting Extreme ($\text{SD}_{\text{cell}} = 0$)
- Consider the thought experiment where $\text{SD}_{\text{cell}} = 0$.
- All 5 cells isolated from Animal 1 yield the exact same value.
- The 15 cell data points in each group are merely **5 identical clones of 3 distinct biological numbers**!
- Any standard t-test on $N \times n = 15$ drastically underestimates true standard error:
  $$\text{SE}_{\text{naive}} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\sqrt{15}} \quad \text{vs.} \quad \text{SE}_{\text{true}} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\sqrt{3}}$$
- The t-statistic is artificially inflated by $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$-fold, causing massive false rejection of the null hypothesis!
:::
:::

## The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Mathematical Formulation
The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient ($\text{ICC}$ or $\rho$) quantifies the proportion of total variance attributable to clustering within animals:

$$\text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{animal}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{animal}} + \sigma^2_{\text{cell}}}$$

- **Range**: $0.0 \le \text{ICC} \le 1.0$.
- **$\text{ICC} \to 1.0$ (High Clustering)**:
  - $\sigma^2_{\text{cell}}$ is very small compared to $\sigma^2_{\text{animal}}$.
  - Cells from the same animal are nearly identical.
  - Extra cells from the same animal provide **zero additional biological information**.
- **$\text{ICC} \to 0.0$ (No Clustering)**:
  - $\sigma^2_{\text{animal}}$ is negligible; variation is dominated by within-cell noise.
  - Cells behave as truly independent samples.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Effective Sample Size ($N_{\text{eff}}$)
Sikkel et al. (2017) and Eisner (2021) formulate the effective sample size for $N$ animals with $n$ cells each:

$$N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{N \times n}{1 + (n - 1) \times \text{ICC}}$$

```{r}
# Display a dynamic lookup table of N_eff
n_cells_grid <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50)
icc_vals <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0)
N_anim <- 3

neff_mat <- outer(n_cells_grid, icc_vals, function(n, r) {
  round((N_anim * n) / (1 + (n - 1) * r), 1)
})
colnames(neff_mat) <- paste0("ICC=", icc_vals)
rownames(neff_mat) <- paste0("n=", n_cells_grid, " cells")
knitr::kable(neff_mat, caption = "Effective Sample Size (N_eff) for N = 3 Animals")
```

::: {.callout-note}
### Key Takeaway
Even with $n = 50$ cells per animal, if $\text{ICC} = 0.5$, your effective sample size is only $5.9$ (not $150$!). When $\text{ICC} = 1.0$, $N_{\text{eff}} \equiv 3.0$.
:::
:::
:::

# Empirical Simulation: "More Means Less" {#simulation-insights background-color="#0f172a"}

## Eisner Figure 1: 3 Animals, 5 Cells per Animal {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Figure 1: Simulation of the effects of comparing 15 cells drawn from 3 animals](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/7594/7814346/d08a6b63a20a/JGP_202012826_Fig1.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### The Dangers of Disaggregation
- **Setup**: Two groups drawn from **identical populations** (Null hypothesis is true: $\Delta \mu = 0$, mean = 1.0; $\text{SD}_{\text{animal}} = 0.3$, $\text{SD}_{\text{cell}} = 0.3$).
- **Panel A ($N = 3$ Animals)**: $t$-test shows no significant difference ($p = 0.15$).
- **Panel B (15 Cells Pooled)**: Naive $t$-test on pooled cells shows highly significant difference ($p = 0.0007$!).

| Statistical Test | Sample Basis | $df$ | $p$-value | Conclusion |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Animal Means** | $N = 3$ / group | $4$ | $0.15$ | Non-significant ✅ |
| **Hierarchical LME** | Random Intercept | $4$ | $0.13$ | Non-significant ✅ |
| **Naive Pooled Test** | $N \times n = 15$ | $28$ | $0.0007$ | **Spurious Positive ❌** |

::: {.callout-caution}
### The 29% False Discovery Rate
Across repeated trials with $\text{SD}_{\text{animal}} = \text{SD}_{\text{cell}} = 0.3$, the naive test yields $p < 0.05$ in **29% of simulations** under the true null!
:::
:::
:::

## Eisner Figure 2: Impact of Animal and Cell SD {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Figure 2: Effects of animal and cell SD on apparent significance](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/7594/7814346/032c8e97a0c0/JGP_202012826_Fig2.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Impact of Variance Components
- **Panel A (Effects of $\text{SD}_{\text{cell}}$)**:
  - Fixed $\text{SD}_{\text{animal}} = 0.3$.
  - Lower $\text{SD}_{\text{cell}}$ ($0.05$, left) tightens cell clusters, yielding $p = 0.001$ ($47\%$ average false positives).
  - Higher $\text{SD}_{\text{cell}}$ ($0.45$, right) widens spread, yielding $p = 0.207$ ($21\%$ false positives).
- **Panel B (Effects of $\text{SD}_{\text{animal}}$)**:
  - Fixed $\text{SD}_{\text{cell}} = 0.3$.
  - Increasing $\text{SD}_{\text{animal}}$ from $0.05$ (left, $p = 0.35$) to $0.45$ (right, $p = 0.002$) escalates false positives from $6\%$ to $37\%$.

::: {.callout-important}
### The Counterintuitive Lesson
Having "cleaner, tighter measurements" with lower technical noise **increases** the false-positive rate if analyzed naively!
:::
:::
:::

## Eisner Figure 3: Cell Count vs. Animal Count {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Figure 3: Dependence of apparent significance on SD and sample numbers](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/7594/7814346/4f208818e241/JGP_202012826_Fig3.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### 200,000-Trial Parameter Sweeps
- **Panel A (2D Parameter Sweep)**:
  - $\text{SD}_{\text{cell}}$ and $\text{SD}_{\text{animal}}$ varied from $0$ to $0.5$ in steps of $0.025$ ($200,000$ trials/condition).
  - **Point A** (low animal SD, high cell SD): nominal $\approx 5\%$.
  - **Point B** (high animal SD, low cell SD): $\mathbf{45\%}$ false positives.
  - **Points C & D** (equal SDs): $\approx \mathbf{35\%}$ false positives.
- **Panel B (Animals vs. Cells)**:
  - Number of animals ($x$-axis) has **almost no effect** on reducing error.
  - Number of cells per animal ($y$-axis) monotonically **escalates false positives** ($>10\%$ at $n=2$, $>40\%$ at $n=8$).

::: {.callout-danger}
### The Takeaway
Studying more than one cell per animal and assuming cells are independent dramatically inflates false discoveries. More means less.
:::
:::
:::

# Four Critical Nuances {#four-nuances background-color="#0f172a"}

## Four Essential Distinctions (Eisner 2021) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### 1. When Cell-Level $n$ IS Valid
- It is entirely valid to use cells as $n$ **when you are not comparing between animals**.
- *Example*: Perfusing an ion channel blocker acutely onto isolated myocytes to measure dose-response kinetics.
- Here, the biological hypothesis pertains to biophysical channel properties across cells, with no between-animal treatment factor.

### 2. Multi-Level Sub-Cellular Nesting
- Often researchers take multiple measurements *within each cell*:
  - Diameters of cellular organelles (mitochondria, granules).
  - Ca2+ sparks recorded in cardiomyocytes (hundreds of sparks per cell!).
- Treating 500 sparks from 3 cells as $N = 1,500$ produces catastrophic pseudoreplication.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### 3. In Vitro Tissue Culture Artifacts
- Cultured cells in dishes or multi-well plates suffer identical clustering:
  - Wells treated with siRNA vs scrambled control.
  - All wells from one flask share passage number, media batch, and incubator position.
  - Treating 6 wells per plate as independent biological replicates is pseudoreplication (Lazic et al., 2018).

### 4. Biological Heterogeneity vs Noise
- Cellular variation within an animal is not always measurement error; it often reflects **real physiological heterogeneity** (e.g., beta-cell metabolic subtypes).
- Hierarchical models allow researchers to model and test changes in **intra-animal dispersion**, rather than discarding it.
:::
:::

## Multi-Tiered Experimental Hierarchies {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
<div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 8px; margin-top: 5px;">
  <div style="background: #0f172a; color: white; padding: 10px 14px; border-radius: 8px; border-left: 5px solid #38bdf8; font-weight: bold; font-size: 0.82em;">
    Tier 1: Experimental Condition / Group (Fixed Treatment Factor)
    <div style="font-size: 0.8em; font-weight: normal; color: #94a3b8; margin-top: 3px;">
      e.g., Wild-Type vs. Transgenic | Control vs. Heart Failure | Drug vs. Vehicle
    </div>
  </div>
  
  <div style="margin-left: 20px; background: #e0f2fe; color: #0369a1; padding: 10px 14px; border-radius: 8px; border-left: 5px solid #0284c7; font-weight: bold; font-size: 0.82em;">
    Tier 2: Animal / Biological Subject (True Experimental Unit: N)
    <div style="font-size: 0.8em; font-weight: normal; color: #0369a1; margin-top: 3px;">
      Random intercept cluster: \(u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\text{animal}})\) • True degrees of freedom (\(N - 2\))
    </div>
  </div>
  
  <div style="margin-left: 40px; background: #fef3c7; color: #b45309; padding: 10px 14px; border-radius: 8px; border-left: 5px solid #d97706; font-weight: bold; font-size: 0.82em;">
    Tier 3: Isolated Cell / Islet / Tissue Slice (Technical Replicate: n)
    <div style="font-size: 0.8em; font-weight: normal; color: #92400e; margin-top: 3px;">
      Residual cell variation: \(\epsilon_{jk} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\text{cell}})\) • Provides NO independent biological df
    </div>
  </div>
  
  <div style="margin-left: 60px; background: #f1f5f9; color: #475569; padding: 10px 14px; border-radius: 8px; border-left: 5px solid #64748b; font-weight: bold; font-size: 0.82em;">
    Tier 4: Subcellular Trace / Organelle (Measurement Replicate: k)
    <div style="font-size: 0.8em; font-weight: normal; color: #64748b; margin-top: 3px;">
      Hundreds of Ca2+ sparks / mitochondria per cell • Extreme pseudoreplication if pooled
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### The Principle of Error Strata
- **Where Treatment Acts**: Experimental conditions are assigned to the **animal** (Tier 2).
- **The Appropriate Error Term**: Hypotheses testing between-group differences must test against variation among **animals**, not subunits nested within them.
- **The Disaggregation Trap**: Pooling Tier 3 or 4 subunits multiplies apparent sample size by $n$ or $k$, producing artificially deflated standard errors and spuriously tiny $p$-values.

::: {.callout-tip}
### The Golden Rule of Degrees of Freedom
Hypotheses comparing **Groups** must be tested against the variance of the units assigned to those groups (**Animals**), never against the variance of subunits nested within them (**Cells**).
:::
:::
:::

# Statistical Solutions {#statistical-solutions background-color="#0f172a"}

## Solution 1: Animal Averaging (Summary Statistics) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### The Simple "Conservative" Approach
- For each animal $i$, compute the arithmetic mean of all its technical replicates:
  $$\bar{y}_i = \frac{1}{n_i} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} y_{ij}$$
- Perform a standard Student's two-sample t-test or one-way ANOVA on the $N$ animal means.
- **Degrees of Freedom**: $\text{df} = N_{\text{total}} - 2$ (e.g., $3 + 3 - 2 = 4$).

::: {.callout-tip}
### The Key Virtue
It completely eliminates pseudoreplication! Under the null hypothesis, the Type I error rate is **guaranteed to be exactly the nominal 5.0%**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Disadvantages & Limitations
::: {.incremental}
1. **Discards Valuable Information**: Strips away intra-animal variance and information on cell-to-cell heterogeneity.
2. **Suboptimal for Unbalanced Designs**:
   - If Animal 1 provided 2 cells and Animal 2 provided 40 cells, simple averaging treats both means as having equal precision.
   - An animal with 2 noisy cells is given the exact same statistical weight as an animal with 40 precise cells!
3. **Loss of Statistical Power**: In unbalanced designs, unweighted averaging reduces statistical power compared to optimal shrinkage estimators.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
### Verdict (Sikkel et al. 2017)
Animal averaging is safe and valid, but mathematically suboptimal when cell counts vary between animals.
:::
:::
:::

## Solution 2: Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMM) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### The Gold Standard Method
Hierarchical linear mixed-effects modeling specifies both fixed treatment effects and random biological clusters:

$$y_{ijk} = \mu + \text{Treatment}_i + u_{j(i)} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

- **$y_{ijk}$**: Measurement for cell $k$ from animal $j$ in group $i$.
- **$\text{Treatment}_i$**: Fixed effect of experimental condition.
- **$u_{j(i)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\text{animal}})$**: Random intercept for animal $j$.
- **$\epsilon_{ijk} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\text{cell}})$**: Residual intra-animal error.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Why LMM is Superior
- Uses **all individual cell measurements**.
- Automatically weights each animal by its precision (effective sample size).
- Completely controls Type I error at nominal 5%.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Shrinkage & Partial Pooling
- In unbalanced datasets, mixed models apply **empirical Bayes shrinkage**:
  - Animal means based on few cells are shrunk toward the overall group mean.
  - Animal means based on many cells remain close to their sample mean.
- **Software Implementation**:
  - **R**: `nlme::lme()`, `lme4::lmer()`.
  - **GraphPad Prism**: "Nested t-test" or "Nested one-way ANOVA" (since Prism v8).
  - **Python**: `statsmodels.formula.api.mixedlm()`.
  - **Julia / Stan**: `MixedModels.jl` or Bayesian hierarchical Stan models.
:::
:::

## Direct Comparison of the Three Approaches {.compact-slide}

| Analytical Feature | Naive Pooled t-test / ANOVA | Animal Averaging (Summary Means) | Hierarchical Linear Mixed Model (LMM) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Data Input Unit** | All individual cells pooled | Mean per animal | All individual cells + Animal ID |
| **Nominal Type I Error ($\alpha = 0.05$)** | **Grossly Inflated (10%–75%) ❌** | **Exact 5.0% ✅** | **Exact 5.0% ✅** |
| **Statistical Power** | Artificially high (spurious) | Valid, but suboptimal if unbalanced | **Optimal (Maximum statistical power) ✅** |
| **Handles Unbalanced Cell Counts?** | No (biases result toward prolific animals) | No (treats $n=2$ same as $n=50$) | **Yes (precision-weighted shrinkage) ✅** |
| **Models Cellular Heterogeneity?** | No | No (discards variance) | **Yes ($\sigma^2_{\text{cell}}$ explicitly estimated) ✅** |
| **Degrees of Freedom Formulation** | $N \times n - 2$ (severely inflated) | $N - 2$ (honest) | Satterthwaite / Kenward-Roger ($N - 2$) |
| **Ease of Execution** | Trivial (Spreadsheet / Basic t-test) | Very Easy (`t.test` on averages) | Moderate (`nlme::lme` or Prism Nested) |

::: {.callout-note}
### Synthesis
When cell numbers per animal are perfectly equal (balanced design), Animal Averaging and Hierarchical LMM give **identical p-values**. When unbalanced, LMM is mathematically superior.
:::

# Case Study: Mouse Islet Cell Hierarchies {#islet-case-study background-color="#0f172a"}

## Alan Attie & Brian Yandell's Islet Discussion {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
### The Laboratory Inquiry (Alan Attie)
> *"We routinely do islet experiments with multiple islet samples from mice. We do the conservative approach of averaging the technical replicates and then doing t-tests or ANOVA with n = number of mice. I wonder if we should be using a hierarchical analysis. What do you think? Can you show me how to do it?"*
> — **Alan** (citing Sikkel et al., 2017)

### Statistical Guidance (Brian Yandell)
> *"Hierarchical analysis gives exactly the same result if nesting is balanced (same number of islets per animal). If not balanced, a weighted analysis would be equivalent. The nesting idea is that islet cells are nested within individuals..."*
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Brian Yandell's Classical ANOVA Table
For $N$ animals and $c$ islets/cells per animal across 2 groups:

$$\begin{array}{lcc}
\hline
\textbf{Source of Variation} & \textbf{Levels} & \textbf{Degrees of Freedom (df)} \\
\hline
\text{Group (Treatment)} & 2 & 1 \\
\text{Individual (Mouse within Group)} & N & N - 2 \\
\text{Islet / Cell (within Mouse)} & N \times c & N(c - 1) \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

::: {.callout-important}
### The Crucial F-Ratio Denominator
In a nested ANOVA, the test for **Group** is:
$$F = \frac{\text{Mean Square}_{\text{Group}}}{\mathbf{\text{Mean Square}_{\text{Mouse}}}}$$
Naive software divides by $\text{Mean Square}_{\text{Within}}$, using $N(c-1)$ degrees of freedom instead of $N-2$!
:::
:::
:::

## Empirical Demonstration: Unbalanced Islet Dataset {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Live Dataset ($N = 8$ Mice, 53 Total Islets)
- Extracted from `data/psuedoreplication.RDS`.
- Control group: Mice have 4, 7, 5, 9 islets.
- Treated group: Mice have 3, 8, 6, 11 islets.

```{r}
#| label: islet-plot
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
d_islet <- sim_data$islet_unbalanced
islet_means <- aggregate(insulin_secretion ~ group + mouse_id, data = d_islet, FUN = mean)

ggplot(d_islet, aes(x = group, y = insulin_secretion, color = mouse_id)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, seed = 2026), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = islet_means, aes(x = group, y = insulin_secretion, fill = mouse_id),
             shape = 23, size = 4.8, stroke = 1.2, color = "black") +
  stat_summary(data = islet_means, aes(x = group, y = insulin_secretion),
               fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.45, color = "black", linewidth = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Mouse Islet Insulin Secretion (Unbalanced)",
    subtitle = "Diamonds = Mouse Means | Dots = Individual Islets",
    x = "", y = "Insulin Secretion (ng / islet / hr)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8fafc", color = NA)
  )
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Side-by-Side Model Outputs in R

```{r}
# 1. Naive pooled model
m_naive <- lm(insulin_secretion ~ group, data = d_islet)
# 2. Averaged mouse model
m_avg <- lm(insulin_secretion ~ group, data = islet_means)
# 3. Hierarchical Linear Mixed Model
m_lme <- nlme::lme(insulin_secretion ~ group, random = ~ 1 | mouse_id, data = d_islet)
```

```r
# 1. NAIVE POOLED LINEAR MODEL (FLAWED)
Residual standard error: 1.834 on 51 degrees of freedom
groupTreated: t = 2.21, p = 0.0315 *  <-- SPURIOUS SIGNIFICANCE!

# 2. CONSERVATIVE MOUSE MEANS (HONEST)
Residual standard error: 1.482 on 6 degrees of freedom
groupTreated: t = 1.15, p = 0.2934    <-- TRUE NULL EFFECT

# 3. HIERARCHICAL LINEAR MIXED MODEL (GOLD STANDARD)
Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML
Fixed effects: groupTreated: Value = 0.582, Std.Error = 0.512, DF = 6
t-value = 1.137, p-value = 0.2988    <-- OPTIMAL UNBIASED INFERENCE
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### Takeaway for Alan
Averaging islet technical replicates works well ($p = 0.293$ vs LME $p = 0.299$). But the naive pooled test falsely claims significance ($p = 0.031$).
:::
:::
:::

# Implementation in R & SuperPlots {#r-workflow background-color="#0f172a"}

## Executable R Code Blueprint {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Classical Nested ANOVA (`aov`)
In base R, specify nested error strata with `+ Error(animal_id)`:

```r
# Balanced or mildly unbalanced nested ANOVA
fit_aov <- aov(
  measurement ~ group + Error(animal_id), 
  data = experiment_data
)
summary(fit_aov)
```
- Produces two separate ANOVA tables:
  1. `Error: animal_id` (tests `group` against animal residual variation with $N-2$ df).
  2. `Error: Within` (reports cell-level residual variation).
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Linear Mixed Models (`nlme` & `lme4`)
The modern standard for nested experimental designs:

```r
# Using base R nlme package
library(nlme)
fit_lme <- lme(
  measurement ~ group, 
  random = ~ 1 | animal_id, 
  data = experiment_data
)
summary(fit_lme)

# Using lme4 & lmerTest for Satterthwaite df
library(lmerTest)
fit_lmer <- lmer(
  measurement ~ group + (1 | animal_id), 
  data = experiment_data
)
anova(fit_lmer)
```
:::
:::

## Best-Practice Visualization: The SuperPlot {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Why Standard Bar Graphs Fail
- Standard bar graphs with error bars (dynamite plungers) hide the underlying data distribution.
- Jittered scatter plots that pool all cells with a single error bar disguise clustering.
- Readers cannot tell whether 60 dots came from 2 animals or 20 animals!

### The SuperPlot Solution (Lord et al., 2020)
1. **Plot every single technical replicate** (cell, islet) as a small, semi-transparent circle.
2. **Color-code by biological replicate** (Animal ID).
3. **Superimpose the biological mean** for each animal as an enlarged diamond or icon.
4. **Display statistical error bars across the biological means ($N$)**, not the pooled cells!
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: superplot-demo
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.8
d1 <- sim_data$eisner_fig1
d1_means <- aggregate(measurement ~ group + animal_id, data = d1, FUN = mean)

ggplot(d1, aes(x = group, y = measurement, color = animal_id)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, seed = 42), size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = d1_means, aes(x = group, y = measurement, fill = animal_id),
             shape = 23, size = 5.5, stroke = 1.3, color = "black") +
  stat_summary(data = d1_means, aes(x = group, y = measurement),
               fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.25, color = "black", linewidth = 1, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(data = d1_means, aes(x = group, y = measurement),
               fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.45, color = "black", linewidth = 0.9, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    title = "SuperPlot of Hierarchical Physiological Data",
    subtitle = "Transparent dots = Cells | Filled diamonds = Animal means | Black bar = Mean ± SE (N=3)",
    x = "Experimental Condition", y = "Physiological Response"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8fafc", color = NA)
  )
```
:::
:::

# Synthesis & Laboratory Guidelines {#synthesis-guidelines background-color="#0f172a"}

## The Physiologist's 5 Cardinal Rules {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note}
### 1. Identify the True Experimental Unit
The experimental unit ($N$) is the smallest entity independently assigned to treatment conditions. Cells from the same animal are technical replicates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
### 2. Never Pool Replicates into Naive t-tests
Never run a two-sample t-test or one-way ANOVA taking sample size as $N \times n$. This inflates false positives up to 50%–75%.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
### 3. Transparently Report Both $N$ and $n$
State explicitly in the manuscript text and figure legends: *"Data represent $n = 53$ islets isolated from $N = 8$ mice ($4$ mice per condition)."*
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-caution}
### 4. Choose Appropriate Software Tools
- If cell counts per animal are balanced: averaging technical replicates and testing animal means with standard t-test is fully valid.
- If cell counts are unbalanced: use Linear Mixed Models (`nlme::lme`, `lmerTest`, GraphPad Prism Nested ANOVA).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
### 5. Present Data with SuperPlots
Display individual cells color-coded by animal, overlaid with animal summary means. Let reviewers and readers see the true degree of clustering.
:::
:::
:::
